prompt: A team splits every item into three and its throughput triples. What does reading cycle time alongside reveal?

choices.why: Right. More, smaller items, the same work delivered.

prompt: Which of Kanban's four measures warns before an item is late?

choices.why: It counts finished items, after the fact.
Right. An item ageing past the 85th percentile is about to become an outlier.

choices.text: Work in progress, as a single total
choices.why: A total does not say which item is ageing.
Measured only once an item is done.

prompt: The team finished 20 items in 28 days with a mean cycle time of 7.75 days. What average work in progress does Little's law imply? Give two decimal places.
At the same throughput, about 0.714 items a day, what mean cycle time would four items in progress give? One decimal place.
The board shows twelve items in progress, but Little's law predicts five. What is the usual cause?
hint: On the board but not worked on.

choices.why: Right. The disagreement points at the cards to look at.

choices.text: Little's law does not apply to software teams at all
choices.why: It applies to any stable system.

choices.text: The team is unusually productive this month
choices.why: Productivity would show in throughput.

prompt: When does Little's law not hold, by the lesson?

choices.text: When items take more than a week
choices.why: Duration does not break it.

choices.text: When the team uses Scrum instead of Kanban
choices.why: The law does not depend on the method.

choices.text: When nobody has estimated the items in points
choices.why: It needs no estimates.

choices.text: While the system is changing fast
choices.why: Right. After a reorganisation or a large batch arriving, the averages are not stable.
